Two corrections to this bead's own description, both worth carrying:
  * _queue_message has TWO drop sites, not one. `return` loses the ARRIVING line; the caller
    thinks it said something. `remove_at(lowest)` loses a WAITING line. The bead and cycle
    90's kanban entry both described only the first.
  * A higher-rung message does NOT evict a queued line. It PRE-EMPTS, which pushes the line
    it interrupted into the queue, and against a full queue of equals that displaced line is
    refused. So the cost of an urgent message is the line the player was mid-way through
    reading, not one they had not reached. The 19-of-22-on-one-rung concern is real but its
    consequence is this, not queue overflow.

NOT by the glob the bead proposed. glob('tools/*_check.py') steps over
tools/check_devtools_log.py, which puts "check" at the FRONT -- it happens to

The rule is the house contract itself: a parallel-safe checker is a tools/*.py
whose source declares a "NOT COVERED:" line. Self-maintaining -- a new checker
written to house-static-checker's contract joins the run when it is saved.

Both exclusion lists are tripwires rather than convenience, per derive-the-list's
"when the hand-typing IS the check" section: NOT_PARALLEL_SAFE (import_check.py,
with the reason) and NOT_A_CHECKER (five entries, each a claim with a reason).
The third category is what makes the derivation total: any tools/*.py that is
neither derived nor listed is reported UNCLASSIFIED and FAILS the run, so a new
tool cannot be silently neither.

Its own first run proved that works by finding one: check_all.py itself, which
owes a NOT COVERED line as a house tool but is a runner, not a checker. It now
has its own SELF branch rather than an entry in a list it would contradict.

Both bead-named exclusions handled deliberately: mirror_check is only ever
invoked read-only (no arg is ever passed, and --fix is the one entry in the
parallel-safe list that WRITES), and run_json_check's exit 2 has a
CONDITIONAL_SKIP entry that PROBES for .devtools/run.json and reports "SKIPPED:
no .devtools/run.json yet -- the normal state at the start of a cycle" while
counting it out of the denominator. Named, not exempted.

THE NURSE BEETLE (Pest.NURSE), campaign waves 17 and 19.

THE QUESTION IT POSES, which is the whole ask. Every damaging plant in this game shoots the
pest FURTHEST ALONG THE ROAD -- the player never picks a target, the rule does. The Nurse
walks behind the front of the queue putting 2.0 health a second back into every other living
pest within 160px. So the garden's own targeting rule will not shoot her while she undoes
the damage that rule is doing.

  The Queen asks: WHERE do I want it to die. Every plant can answer her.
  The Nurse asks: does my garden own anything that can hit the BACK of a wave.

The only two answers are the two plants that ignore the furthest-along rule -- a Chomp at
the mouth of a lane, and a Dandelion whose blast lands on an area. It is the breadth-vs-depth
question with teeth: eleven level-1 cobs at 1.25 dps each never finish anything inside the
aura, however many there are, unless two are on the same pest.

Not a bigger Queen: 48 health against her 80, no split, and she is the only boss that
HURRIES (speed 44, faster than the beetle column she is scheduled behind).

EVERY NUMBER DERIVED. The heal rate sits between one level-1 cob's 1.25/s and twice it, with
a maxed cob at its rim (2.26/s) just clearing it -- both ends asserted against
CornCobbler.LEVELS rather than written down. One pulse is exactly one whole aphid, so a
swarm inside the aura visibly stops dying. The radius is under CornCobbler.RANGE (so a cob
that can see her can reach everything she protects) and under the 192px between parallel
road rows (so an aura never leaks into a lane she is not in). Her health is set so two maxed
cobs do not take her and three do, from the chord across a cob's ring at her speed. Her seed
value is 39 because CompostMeter.husk_value_for times the four composable mutation
multipliers turns it into four husks, and in the whole band 24..40 only 39 and 40 leave
every droppable husk tellable from every other.

THE ARITHMETIC, and it displaced NOTHING. Waves 17 and 19 each lose 3 beetles and gain 1
Nurse: 48 points out, 48 back in, both times. Every wave from 1 to 300 prices to the number
it did before, the seam bound is still 436.7, and the finale is byte-for-byte the row it has
always been -- unmoved for the fourth species running. A Nurse in the finale would have cost
48 of its 18.7 points of headroom, i.e. illegal outright rather than merely expensive.

The offline replica was validated BEFORE use (it reproduced the golden array, the 2112px
route, the 40-of-40 finale peak, 418 base health, the 436.7 bound and strict threat rise to
wave 300) and then re-run against the edited source PARSED BACK OUT of the files rather than
retyped.

THE COMMANDS, recorded so they can be re-run:
    python .claude/surveys/heredoc_survey.py            # the sweep

RESULT: 933 (commit, .gd file) versions across 631 commits and all branches. Signature A (a string literal containing a literal newline) = 0. Signature B (comment prose with no leading #) = 0.

THE ZERO IS LOAD-BEARING, so it is controlled. A sweep that reports 0 and a sweep that is broken read identically, and this one was broken twice before it was right:
  - v1 scanned diff LINES and reported 554 hits, ALL FALSE -- every one a prose comment in which a quoted phrase wrapped across two # lines. Counting quotes per line cannot tell a broken string from a sentence.
  - v2 used a hand-rolled (?<!\)" regex and reported 144 hits, ALL FALSE -- every one an 'if c == "\\\\":' in the test suite, because that regex does not know an escaped backslash is not an escaped quote.
  - v3 asks tools/gdsource.py's literal_spans instead, which is the same scanner pass that does the blanking and therefore cannot disagree with it. 0.
The control file pins all four outcomes: it fires on real Signature A damage, fires on real Signature B damage, and stays silent on both false-positive classes above. 5 of 5 pass. So the zero is a measurement, not an absence of measurement.

DECISION: NO CHECKER, and the count is the justification. house-static-checker's denominator rule wants evidence the defect happens; the denominator is 0 in 933. More useful than the number is WHY it is zero -- there are two escape paths and both already terminate in a parser. Damage to GDScript is caught by lint/import/compile; damage to the scratch script doing the editing is caught by Python's own parser. Neither can be silent for long, which is exactly what the five known incidents show: all were caught the same day.

SIXTH OCCURRENCE, observed live, and it is the first one caught IN THE ACT rather than reconstructed: while writing this very survey I patched it through 'python - <<PY', the heredoc ate the backslash in every "\n", and the escape became a literal newline inside a string literal -- an unterminated string at the exact line the patch touched. That is precisely the cycle-97 shape (a Python script inside a heredoc, shell plus a second escaping layer), reproduced by the person surveying how often it happens, one hour after quoting the rule to two lanes. Python's SyntaxError caught it within one command.

So the rule in CLAUDE.md step 2 EARNS ITS KEEP -- it saves real time -- but it does not need a tool behind it. Its value is avoiding the loop, not preventing a silent defect, because a silent one has never been demonstrated here and the survey now says so with a denominator.

Decided, per surface, by measuring rather than by defaulting. Written up in .claude/corpus-checking-verdict.md.

THE RULE THE MEASURING TURNED UP, which is the real deliverable because it answers the NEXT surface too: what a surface does when text overflows decides whether it needs a corpus.
  - WRAPS -> the overflow goes into HEIGHT, and any clearance or stack-height gate catches it for free.
  - GROWS/PUSHES -> it goes into LAYOUT, and a layout budget catches it.
  - CLIPS (clip_text + OVERRUN_TRIM_ELLIPSIS) -> it goes NOWHERE. It becomes an ellipsis. Height and layout are unchanged, so no existing gate has any second-order effect to notice. Only this case needs a content corpus.

That is why 'has not broken yet' means different things on different surfaces: a wrapping surface that has not broken has been tested by every layout gate that ever ran; a clipping one has not been looked at.

THE COROLLARY IS THE SHARP END. clip_text is exactly what makes Label.get_minimum_size() report ~1px -- it returns the clip stub, not the text -- so assert_gte(label.size.x, get_minimum_size().x) passes UNCONDITIONALLY on precisely the labels that need checking. The surfaces that most need a corpus are the ones where a careless gate looks like it is already there. The project has applied the fix once (the notebook hints page uses _T.text_width and says why); it has not been applied to the run summary.

PER SURFACE:
  * STATS ROW -- COVERED, do not build. hud_readouts walks WORST_CASE_TEXT and measures each declared worst case in the real theme font against its slot: that IS the corpus pattern, already applied. hud_stats_row prices the layout so a new child is noticed even if undeclared. MEASURED: 4 labels in the live row (Seeds/Wave/Lives/Compost), 4 keys in WORST_CASE_TEXT -- complete today. One small gap: every assertion iterates the DICTIONARY, never the row, so a readout added without a declared worst case is not reported as uncovered (the reverse direction IS handled). Worth one assertion next time someone is in that file; not worth its own bead.
  * SELECTION PANEL -- was the open question, now answered empirically and it is the strongest evidence here. It had 'comments and one hand measurement', the same standing as the run summary, and -r722 priced it this cycle at 0 px of vertical room with TWO lines already past the box. So for one of three surfaces, 'has not broken yet' was nobody looking. It was already over, and it stayed quiet because the panel WRAPS -- the overflow went into height, where nothing was measuring.
  * RUN SUMMARY -- BUILD IT. run_summary.gd sets clip_text + OVERRUN_TRIM_ELLIPSIS on title, note and value labels. So a too-long value clips rather than wraps; size.y does not change; and the only gate on the surface is BUTTON_CLEARANCE, which compares label.position.y + label.size.y against the replay button -- it reads a height a content regression cannot move, so it is STRUCTURALLY INCAPABLE of firing on one. Confirmed by grep across all three suite files: ZERO width assertions on the run summary's Value_* labels. That is this bead's own build condition met exactly: 'only build where the answer is nothing would notice'.

The run-summary verdict is the justification -wf4i should cite; noted there, with the two traps whoever takes it will hit.

ALSO USEFUL TO THE QUEUE: -ox1p found this group is 15 of 90 open beads, the largest by half again. The rule above is a stopping condition for the application beads in it -- a surface earns a corpus when it CLIPS -- which is checkable in one grep of the surface's file rather than by re-arguing each from scratch.

Across three runs at the same step size the peak was always step 3 and always 0.880, but the APPROACH differed each time (0.953/0.917/0.880 in one run, 0.927/0.903/0.880 in another). So a check that reads one fixed step index is measuring the harness's stepping behaviour rather than the tween. WALK PAST THE PEAK AND TAKE THE EXTREME.

I SHARPENED THE BEAD'S PROPOSED RULE, and this is the part worth keeping. The bead asked to flag 'both sides are Objects with the same instance id'. That would FALSE-POSITIVE on a legitimate identity assertion -- asserting a getter handed back the node you gave it is a real test, and the two sides are the same object by design. The narrowed rule is: same object AND already freed. Two references to one dangling object cannot fail for any reason a test intended; two references to one live object can.

THE JUDGEMENT THE BEAD FLAGGED. There is no property in this project that distinguishes a loss from a gain -- Sfx knows a file, a volume, a pitch, a wobble and a repeat gap, and none has a sign; the call sites share no marker; lives is a bare int with no signal. Three derivations were tried and REJECTED, each recorded so the next reader does not re-try them:
  1. the sign of PITCH itself -- the table agreeing with itself, which is the defect not the check;
  2. the '# Losses, gravest first' comments already in sfx.gd -- a comment IS the prose being escaped;
  3. cost in seeds, the only currency spanning both columns -- and it prices PLANT_UPGRADED as a LOSS, because upgrading is the one entry the player pays for. A derivation that produces the wrong answer confidently is worse than no derivation.

So this took derive-the-list's step-1 branch: a taste call gets recorded rather than derived. Sfx.PITCH_GRADE now sits below PITCH with a SIGNED RANK per event, not a boolean -- and the rank is the point. A boolean would be a bit-for-bit copy of sign(pitch - 1.0) and the test would agree with itself; a rank also carries the gravity ORDERING, which the pitch numbers state nowhere. The two sides are the author's stated intent and the tuned number, neither computed from the other, so retuning a pitch without moving its rank goes red.

What it still cannot say, and both files say so: whether the intent is right. Nobody has heard these numbers.

FIVE MUTATIONS PLANTED, ALL RED, EACH FOR A DIFFERENT REASON, with a green control first: an entry added to PITCH and left ungraded; an entry graded a loss but pitched up; a PITCH row deleted leaving a stray grade (the direction a one-sided 'has' check cannot fail); a retune that keeps the sign but breaks the gravity ordering; and giving RUN_LOST a pitch row when it is alone on its file and so has no base to be heard against. The last two kill mutations the old one-pair check could never have seen.

RELATIONSHIP between a sentence and code elsewhere, and there is no shared vocabulary
between them to check -- "hungry", "shoots", "idle" are English, not identifiers.

SHIPPED. `--snapshot` / `--against` on tools/citation_check.py, wired into the cycle skill's
step 3.

CLAUSE BY CLAUSE.

"both modes exist" -- yes. `--snapshot PATH` records what every RESOLVED citation lands on,
normalised for leading whitespace (indentation moves for reasons unrelated to the claim; a
block re-indented under a new `if` is not a citation going stale). `--against PATH`
re-resolves and reports the ones whose text moved, printing `was:` and `now:`.

"a synthetic fixture proves the check FAILS on a citation whose target moved and PASSES on
one that did not -- both directions" -- both run, both correct:
  * POSITIVE: insert one line above a cited line -> `DRIFTED: game/bramble.gd:120-120 /
    was: super.take_damage(amount * bite_resistance()) / now: func take_damage(...)`, exit 1.
  * NEGATIVE: nothing moved -> `0 drifted`, exit 0. Reverting the insertion -> exit 0 again.
  * Plus a third: `--against` with no snapshot file is exit 2, not a clean "0 drifted". A
    report of zero against a file that does not exist is indistinguishable from having
    checked, which is what every NOT COVERED line in this repo exists to prevent.

"new citations are reported separately from drifted ones" -- yes, as NEW, and they do not
gate. An entry written this cycle has nothing to compare against.

"the existing 351-citation run is unchanged when no snapshot is given" -- byte-identical:
`351 citation(s) across 1 file(s), 351 resolved, 0 finding(s)`, exit 0. check_all still 19
of 19 clean.

THREE THINGS THE WORK TURNED UP, none of which was the feature:

1. CONFIRMING THE PREMISE STOPPED ME OVERLOADING AN EXISTING FLAG. citation_check ALREADY
   has --baseline / --baseline-write and I nearly reused them. They snapshot FINDINGS,
   answering "which broken citations are new". Drift is about citations that still RESOLVE.
   One flag meaning both would have made a clean --baseline run read as evidence about
   drift, which it is not. The bead specified --snapshot/--against and was right to.

2. THE NEW MODE'S DENOMINATOR CONTRADICTED THE TOOL'S OWN: 310 against 351. Correct -- the
   map is keyed by file:start-end, so a target cited from two entries collapses to one --
   but printing only the smaller number beside a default run saying 351 reads as 41
   citations gone missing. Both numbers now print in both modes.

3. THE FIRST FIXTURE WAS VACUOUS AND SAID SO. An absolute Windows path's drive colon
   (C:/Users/...) is not matched by the CITATION regex, so it reported "0 citation(s), 0
   resolved" and BOTH controls would have passed over nothing. Caught by reading the
   denominator on the SETUP run rather than on the assertion -- which is the whole argument
   for printing one.

WIRED, NOT JUST WRITTEN. Step 3 of the cycle skill now carries the snapshot-before /
check-after pair with the reason. Cycle 111's entire lesson was that .claude/surveys/ held

DECIDED AND PINNED. The answer is NO: a 60-seed husk keeps the same 4.5s floor as a 9-seed
one.

THE PREMISE HELD, and re-deriving it independently is what made it safe to build on.
Pest.SPECIES crossed with every composable multiplier gives ten reachable values --
{2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 14, 20, 30, 40, 60} -- six of them at or above FULL_VALUE (9), all getting
lifetime_for == MIN_HUSK_LIFETIME == 4.5s. Same ten the bead lists, computed from the
species table rather than copied from it.

THE BEAD'S QUESTION WAS HALF-ANSWERED ALREADY, and finding that changed what this cycle
did. FULL_VALUE's own comment reads: "FULL_VALUE stays at 9 deliberately. It is the knob
lifetime_for was tuned against, so widening it to 60 would silently slow the rot of every
husk in the game -- a balance change wearing a legibility fix's clothes."

That settles the KNOB. It says nothing about whether rot should distinguish above 9 by some
OTHER means -- a second curve with its own ceiling, say -- which is what the bead actually
asked. So this cycle recorded the decision with its own reasons rather than re-deriving a
constraint that was already written down.

THE DECISION, with the reasoning, now above MIN_HUSK_LIFETIME:

  1. 4.5s IS A REACTION TIME, NOT A DIFFICULTY KNOB. The values above 9 come from the two
     bosses -- Pest.SPECIES puts the Nurse Beetle at 39 seeds and the Queen at 40 -- crossed
     with mutations. So the richest husks drop at the single busiest moment on the board: a
     health bar emptying, plants firing, lives possibly just spent. Going below this makes
     the rarest drop the hardest to claim, which punishes the player at the game's high
     point rather than making it tense.
  2. THE URGENCY IS ALREADY CARRIED, TWICE, above the saturation point -- size and glow to
     9, and HuskLayer.overflow_pips counting beyond it. A player already knows a 60 is
     special. What they do not need is less time to act on knowing.
  3. THE FAILURES ARE NOT SYMMETRIC. Rot too slow and the compost meter is mildly too
     generous. Rot too fast on exactly the rarest drops and the player learns that boss
     kills are not worth chasing -- the opposite of what a boss should teach.

THE INCONSISTENCY THE BEAD NAMES IS ACCEPTED, NOT DENIED. "The pips now say one is worth six
times the other while the clock says hurry equally" is true. The pips answer "how much is
this worth" and the clock answers "how long do you have"; those are different questions and
they are allowed to saturate differently, because value is unbounded and reaction time is
not.

PINNED IN THREE PARTS, and the third is the one that makes it a gate rather than a comment.
test_the_rot_floor_is_a_floor_and_the_curve_still_sorts_below_it asserts:
  * nothing rots faster than the floor, at every reachable value AND at 999 and 100000;
  * everything at or above FULL_VALUE shares the floor, with a non-vacuous count guard;
  * BELOW FULL_VALUE a richer husk rots STRICTLY faster.

The third exists because the first two are BOTH satisfiable by flattening the curve
entirely: making every husk rot at 4.5s would "fix" the inconsistency and pass them.
Confirmed by mutation -- HUSK_LIFETIME = MIN_HUSK_LIFETIME fires only the ordering
assertion, and widening FULL_VALUE to 60 fires only the saturation-count guard. A decision
pinned only where it holds is not pinned.

The reachable values are DERIVED inside the test from Pest.SPECIES rather than listed, so a
new species or a new multiplier moves this with the game instead of leaving it asserting a
table nobody updated.

WHAT IS NOT DONE, deliberately: no balance change. Nothing about the curve, the floor,
FULL_VALUE or the pips moved. The bead said it was "filed so the question is on the record,
not so it gets built", and the answer turned out to be that the current behaviour is right

MEASURED AND DECIDED. The ring stays; nothing is suppressed.

BOTH DURATIONS, as the acceptance asked, and all five rather than two.
Pest.SPECIES chew_seconds: aphid 0.45, beetle 2.6, Shield Bug 3.0, Nurse Beetle 5.0,
Queen 11.0. MUTATION_ARMOURED doubles any of them, so the real range the ring must work
across is 0.45s to 22s.

The number the bead did not have: the aphid is 5.8x shorter than the next one up. It is not
merely the shortest, it is in a different league from every other case -- and it is the
commonest pest in the game.

THE DECISION: NO SUPPRESSION. Three reasons, and the third is the one that settles it.

1. THE RING MEANS BUSY. A Chomp mid-chew cannot grab anything (is_busy() is `_held != null`)
   and the ring is what says so. Suppress it below a threshold and a busy Chomp reads as a
   FREE one for exactly as long as the suppression lasts -- at the moment a player is most
   likely to be scanning for a mouth to throw the next pest at. The bead framed this as
   "is the flash readable"; the more important question is what its ABSENCE says, and its
   absence already means something.

2. IT WOULD HIDE THE MAJORITY CASE. The aphid is the pest the player sees most, so any
   threshold above 0.45s removes the ring from most chews in the game -- leaving a cue too
   rare for anyone to learn, which is a worse outcome than a brief one.

3. THE SHOP ALREADY PROMISED THE FLASH. PlantCatalog's Chomp entry reads: "Eats small pests
   instantly. Big ones take a while -- and it is busy the whole time." A 0.45s sweep reading
   as instantaneous is not a cue failing. It is the cue agreeing with the sentence the
   player was sold before they bought the plant. The ring exists for "big ones take a
   while", and there it has 2.6 to 22 seconds to work in.

That third point is what reframed the item. The bead's premise -- "a design question nobody
has asked" -- was not quite right: it had been answered, in the shop line, and nothing
checked that the answer was still true of the numbers.

SO THE DELIVERABLE IS A RELATIONSHIP, NOT TWO RECORDED NUMBERS. The acceptance asked for
"both chew durations recorded as numbers"; recorded numbers go stale, and this file has
spent several cycles removing exactly that shape.
test_the_chomps_shop_line_is_true_of_the_chew_table derives them from SPECIES and pins all
three clauses of the blurb:
  * the quickest meal is the SMALLEST pest -- not merely some pest. If the Queen were ever
    fastest to eat, the sentence would be false while every duration in it stayed the same.
  * every other species takes at least 4x the aphid's chew. A RELATIVE gap deliberately,
    because "instant" is a fact about perception and no test here can measure one; what it
    can measure is that the two halves of the sentence describe two different experiences.
  * a Chomp is busy for even the quickest meal, with chew progress left to draw -- which is
    the assertion that makes the no-suppression decision structural rather than a comment.

Mutation-tested: aphid 0.45 -> 1.2 fires the gap assertion naming both durations.

SHIPPED. A binding that did not reach disk now says so, on the screen, in words a player can
act on.

THE PREMISE HELD EXACTLY. RunConfig._save() was `-> void` with four failure paths --
FileAccess.open returning null, a short write, a readback that does not parse, and a failed
rename -- each reporting via push_warning and nothing else. push_warning reaches the editor
log, which a player does not have and a screen cannot read. So KeyBindingScreen._persist()
wrote on every capture and the only feedback was the row's key text changing, which is
identical whether or not the write landed.

THE CHANGE. _save() returns whether the record reached disk; store_key_bindings and
_persist() thread it to the two places that can say something (a capture and the reset). All
13 other _save() callers ignore it and are still correct -- they had no answer before and the
behaviour on failure is unchanged.

TWO JUDGEMENTS, and neither is obvious until you have to write the sentence:

1. THE RENAME FAILURE RETURNS TRUE. Its own warning reads "The finished save is at %s and
   _load will adopt it" -- the record is complete, validated, and on disk; the next launch
   picks it up. Three of the four paths lose the write and return false. This one does not.
   A save confirmation that claims work was lost when it was not is worse than no
   confirmation at all, and that failure direction is the one a player cannot recover from
   by ignoring it.

2. THE SUCCESS SENTENCE SAYS NOTHING. "Set: M sound effects on or off" is what a player
   wants to read. Appending "saved" to every capture would put a word about disks on a
   screen about keys, forever, to cover a case that essentially never happens. Silence is the
   confirmation; the failure is what needs words.

   That asymmetry is also what made this testable: persisted_note() returns its caller's own
   sentence UNCHANGED on success, so both branches are pure and assertable with no screen,
   no save file and no failing disk.

THE FINDING WORTH READING, because the obvious implementation is wrong and looks right:

Mouse emulation stays ON deliberately -- every Button in this game is a Control answering
mouse events, so turning it off to get clean touch handling would kill the shop, the pause
card and every Back button on exactly the devices this is for. So the engine sends BOTH
events for one finger, and the whole job is telling them apart.

The obvious way is a flag set by the touch handler. It cannot work, and a probe on the
running game is what showed that:

    PROBE mouse press  device=-1  touch_index=-1
    PROBE screen touch pressed index=0 device=0

The emulated mouse press arrives BEFORE the InputEventScreenTouch that produced it. The
first implementation therefore planted at the PRESS cell -- the exact defect
commit-on-release exists to remove -- and no ordering of the branches in _unhandled_input
fixes it.

The discriminator is the device id: Godot marks the emulated event -1 and a real one 0.
Narrowed by DisplayServer.is_touchscreen_available() on purpose, because -1 means
SYNTHESISED rather than "from touch" -- the devtools bridge's own mouse-move sends one, and
on a desktop with no touchscreen a -1 event is a test driving the game and must be honoured.

WHAT THE HEADLESS TEST CANNOT COVER, stated because it is unusual: the emulated-mouse guard.
is_touchscreen_available() is a property of the machine, not something a test can set. So
the bridge check is genuinely covering a different half rather than re-confirming the suite
-- the one clear case of that this session.

THE TASTE CALL WAS TAKEN AS WRITTEN and is the whole design: rungs buy RESISTANCE, not
health. A heal is worth 1 / (EAT_DPS * bite_resistance()) seconds, so lowering the
resistance scales the Salve Aloe standing behind the wall -- and the rain -- WITH the
upgrade. A bigger pool would dilute both, making the board this plant exists to create worse
as you invest in it.

equally true of the pool version the bead argued against. It compares what one second of
Aloe healing is worth at the bottom rung against the top, and is mutation-tested by
flattening the resistances, which is exactly what a pool ladder looks like from here.

MY DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG. --snapshot-userstate is INNOCENT. The real defect is in this project's own save code, it is worse than what I filed, and it is fixed.

WHAT I FILED (cycle 133): "--snapshot-userstate stops the game saving." Evidence was a paired run -- with the flag, `_save()` returned false and the file never changed; without it, true and the file changed.

WHY THAT WAS WRONG. The pairing was real and the attribution was not. Re-run with the ORDER REVERSED -- plain launch first, flagged launch second -- and `_save()` returns TRUE under the flag, twice. The flag does not touch user:// writability at all: `userstate_snapshot` (tools/devtools.py:1835) COPIES matching files into `.devtools/` with `shutil.copy2` and holds nothing open. I should have read that before filing at P1, and the bead's own acceptance told me to ("read the harness implementation FIRST"). I filed instead.

THE REAL TRIGGER, found by replaying cycle 133's exact call sequence under the flag:

    record_milestones(["SNAPSHOT_PROBE"])  -> ["SNAPSHOT_PROBE"]   (reported as recorded)
    _save()                                -> FALSE
    toggle_mute_sfx()                      -> true
    _save()                                -> FALSE

An UNKNOWN MILESTONE ID BREAKS EVERY SUBSEQUENT SAVE IN THE SESSION. `MILESTONE_ID_CHARS` (game/run_config.gd:146) is lowercase, digits and underscore. `_parse_milestones` rejects any token containing anything else. `_save()` writes the file and then reads it back through the loader's own validator -- deliberately, and its comment says why: "so a future writer that its own reader cannot read fails here, loudly, instead of at some player's next launch." It does fail. But the bad id is still sitting in `earned_milestones`, so it fails again on the next save, and the next. The player's high score, settings and real milestones all quietly stop persisting.

And the reporting is split, which is what made it cost most of a cycle to attribute: `_save()` warns and returns false, while `record_milestones()` has already returned the id as freshly recorded. The caller is told it succeeded.

THE FIX, in game/run_config.gd: `record_milestones` now refuses an id that cannot round-trip, at the door, with a push_warning naming the legal character set -- the same shape as the hint refusal directly above it, which exists for the same reason. The predicate is `is_recordable_milestone(id)`, and it is DERIVED from `MILESTONE_ID_CHARS` rather than restating the rule, because the two halves being written independently is exactly how a writer comes to accept what its own reader rejects.

THE DETAIL THAT MAKES IT WORK, and the lane found it rather than being told: close() NOT queue_free() at the close paths. queue_free defers to end of frame, so an _exit_tree restore lands AFTER the opener's grab_focus() — and grab_focus() on a FOCUS_NONE control is an error, not a focus. _exit_tree stays as a backstop for Game.resume_run() freeing the whole pause layer with an overlay still open.

The cover set is DERIVED from the tree rather than kept as a list, with the overlay's own subtree skipped so it can never kill its own Back button. And the hold is idempotent per control, which is exactly what lets TitleScreen._set_menu_active keep running alongside without its redundant calls turning the release into a no-op — that is why title_screen was left untouched rather than half-converted.

THE DECISION: a move PRESERVES the plant -- same node, level, health -- and
costs a quarter of what the player has put in (base cost plus every seed spent
climbing), floored at 1 and rounded up. Four moves cost you the plant.

WHY NOT THE PRICE THIS BEAD PROPOSED. It framed the choice as free / full /
refund-minus-cost, and called the third the middle. Refund-minus-cost is FOUR
SEEDS on a healthy Corn Cobbler -- the free option with extra arithmetic. The
bead's own diagnosis ("the move preview shows them a decision the game then
charges them full price to act on") was right about the symptom and wrong about
the cause: the seeds were never the barrier. commit_uproot() frees the plant, so
a move destroyed the LEVEL, and uproot_refund() scales the BASE cost. A fully
climbed cob cost 10 - 6 + 65 forfeited AND the climb again, to shift one cell.
The cost of moving scaled with how much the player cared about the plant.

So the price is only half the answer and the preservation is the other half.
Measured live on a climbed cob: 8 seeds to move against 24 to uproot and rebuy.

Gated on the armed window rather than a new mode: arm_uproot already selects the
plant, starts the clock and turns on the destination preview the move tip tells

Built tools/teaching_ledger_check.py; check_all 21 -> 22. THE LEDGER HAD DRIFTED AGAIN, on a different row and in the same direction: row 6 read 'untaught' while HINT_DEFERRED_ROAD (cycle 144) and HINT_DEAD_GROUND (cycle 151) both taught its two bars -- and cycle 151 read that very block while shipping the second of them. The bead's own example, row 4, had already been fixed by hand; the drift it predicted was live somewhere else. Corrected. THE CHECKABLE DIRECTION NEEDED A NEW KEY: nothing in the codebase recorded which grammar row a hint teaches, so Hud.HINT_CARDS entries now carry grammar_row (0 for the four hints that teach a RULE rather than a mark). Without it a tool can confirm a TAUGHT row names something real but cannot confirm an 'untaught' row is unclaimed -- which is the only direction that has ever actually drifted here. GATING rather than advisory, deliberately: every finding has one correct response, so a red run is always actionable and can never become permanent. Two mutations: reverting row 6 produced the finding naming both hints; disabling the grammar_row read made it vanish while the ledger was still wrong. NOT COVERED is explicit that the TAUGHT direction is counted rather than matched -- the ledger names rows in prose and CueLegend.ROWS names them by SHAPE const, and deciding those are the same row is judgement, not lookup.
